title: Innovating While Scaling: Lessons from Amazon
summary:
What can today's startups learn from Amazon's so-called, quote, invention machine and the culture of growth and innovation there that led to several successful and diverse lines of products? As it scaled, how did Amazon define and adapt its culture and practices to promote innovation even as it got more complex and large? It's all based on their book,
working backwards, Insight, Stories, and Secrets from Inside Amazon, drawing upon the 27 years
of the combined experience they had of being in the room where it happened at Amazon.

thesis: This episode argues that Amazon's success stems from a rigorous 'working backwards' process that forces customer-centricity from the initial idea stage, often requiring extensive iteration and PRFAQ documents before greenlighting projects. It further posits that the company scaled by breaking into loosely coupled teams with a services-based architecture while maintaining a culture that prioritizes long-term growth and customer value over short-term quarterly results.

claims.claim: Amazon uses a working backwards process starting from the customer perspective to ensure the customer is front and center from the very first iteration of an idea.
claims.quote: At its heart, the working backwards process is really starting from the customer perspective and everything you do works backwards from that. The PRFAQ, the press release and FAQ, that is the tool that Amazon uses to achieve the perspective of starting from the customer.

claims.claim: Amazon deliberately uses mechanisms to ensure the customer is front and center from the very first iteration of an idea.
claims.quote: Amazon has put in deliberate mechanisms to make sure that the customer is front and center from the very first iteration of an idea.

claims.claim: Amazon uses PRFAQ documents, consisting of a press release and frequently asked questions, as a tool to achieve the perspective of starting from the customer.
claims.quote: The PRFAQ, the press release and FAQ, that is the tool that Amazon uses to achieve the perspective of starting from the customer.

claims.claim: Amazon's working backwards process involves writing up ideas as press releases and FAQs before getting greenlit after several iterations.
claims.quote: And what that is, it's two things. It's a press release and then a frequently asked questions document. And the press release has to clearly explain to the customer what it is. you're building, what's the problem you're trying to solve for the customer, and why does it make their life better?

claims.claim: Amazon's PRFAQ documents are an iterative process where most ideas do not make it out and several iterations and feedback are needed before the project gets greenlit.
claims.quote: First of all, most of the ideas that go through it don't make it out on the other side. And second is that it takes several, several iterations and feedback to refine before the project gets greenlit.

claims.quote: For perspective, at the end of 2003, 73, 77% of all of Amazon's worldwide revenue was media products, but it was all physical media products.

claims.claim: Amazon had a digital media team in 2004 when the speaker landed on a new role working as one of the founding members.
claims.quote: in 2004, I landed on a new role working as one of the founding members of the digital media team in Amazon.

claims.claim: Amazon tried mock-ups for a little while but there were so many questions and so many details that they hadn't thought out.
claims.quote: We tried mock-ups for a little while, but frankly, there was sort of like so many questions and so many details that we hadn't thought out.

claims.claim: Amazon employees wrote up ideas for what they think they should go build in digital, including a puck that would sit on your countertop and you would talk to the puck and could order groceries from the puck.
claims.quote: We'll write those things up and we'll come back. in a few days and we'll read those and we'll go from there. And this is before we had done narratives. We had not figured out this PRFAQ concept yet. But once we did that, everything changed. claims.claim: Some of the documents describing ideas for digital music or Kindle became eight pages long.
claims.quote: Another one was describing an early version of what Kindle might become. But some of these documents are like eight pages long.

claims.claim: Amazon successfully solved the problem of scaling by breaking up into loosely coupled teams and adopting a services-based architecture.
claims.quote: came up with a different answer. Some companies would say, let's build coordination tools, let's collaborate better. And Jeff said, I'd love to eliminate coordination altogether. Now, in practice, you can't eliminate it completely. So you break up into loosely coupled teams. And this was a hard, hard problem to solve because it required to change the way we built Amazon. claims.claim: Amazon prioritized long-term growth and customer value over short-term quarterly results, exemplified by the launch of Amazon Prime during the holiday season.
claims.quote: Amazon Prime, he made the call that, hey, we're going to go launch this shipping project in the holiday season. And it was not very popular at the time. But when he explained his thinking that, you know, customers were basically giving us a B minus on our three to five day shipping, even though we had just gotten reasonably competent and spent a couple of $100 million doing that.

claims.claim: Jeff Bezos focused top leaders on the biggest opportunities, such as AWS and digital, even when they had zero revenue initially.
claims.quote: One of the enlightening things that I realized during my time with Jeff is what he chose to work on during the two years, I was his shadow or technical advisor. And it wasn't the biggest businesses at Amazon. About half of the time were spent on what would become AWS and digital. And those businesses had revenue of effectively zero for the, you know, those two years.

claims.claim: Amazon's leadership principles are core to its culture, with leaders holding themselves and others accountable to high standards.
claims.quote: insist on high, on the highest standards is one of Amazon's leadership principles. He holds people accountable, himself included, by the way. And I would say that I also learn that sticking to these core principles is harder than it sounds.

claims.claim: Amazon's evolution into a complex system of modular, self-contained units allowed it to thrive and remain agile.
claims.quote: And you're essentially describing how modular self-contained units can thrive in these complex systems. It's a lot like evolution. And these pieces all fit together because then we have to look back to like, oh, the reason that Amazon could do that is because those teams wrote narratives in PRFAQ, so they made it abundantly clear.
